newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland arms plan faces defeat, talks mired.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland arms plan faces defeat, talks mired.

text.p: Anglo-Irish proposals that Northern Ireland guerrillas disarm while pursuing peace talks faced defeat on Wednesday, casting a cloud over plans to forge an end to decades of conflict.

Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, said she expected the "parallel decommissioning" proposals to be voted down when parties to the talks are balloted on 50-odd amendments to the plan on Wednesday.
"It's not a disaster, it is clearly a setback but no one ever said this would be easy," Mowlam told reporters a few hours before participants in the multi-party talks began voting in mid-afternoon.

Defeat would leave unresolved the single most contentious issue in a peace process launched in December 1993, and throw into doubt plans to begin substantive negotiations on a lasting settlement by the two governments' target date of September 15.
Mowlam said that even if the proposals were voted down, the two governments would maintain their target date of September 15 to begin talks on a settlement.
"What I want is peace and the way we will get that is through inclusive talks...I'm not prepared in an interview now to reject the present format which has taken years to build," she said.

But political sources said failure to agree how and when guerrillas could disarm might torpedo chances of getting the unionists and Sinn Fein, political wing of Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas, to the same negotiating table.
David Trimble, leader of the most powerful Protestant group, the Ulster Unionist Party, said he would probably vote against the proposals but would not leave the negotiations.
Trimble wants the talks underpinned by a decommissioning plan that would commit Sinn Fein and its Protestant loyalist extremist foes to handing over weapons during the talks.

The British and Irish governments reply that the proposals, framed as a compromise after more than a year of stalemate, say guerrillas should disarm during the talks. Trimble wants the wording of any plan to say that they must.

He and fellow unionist parties, two of which have said they are walking out of the negotiations after Wednesday's vote, believe that last weekend's IRA ceasefire is just a ruse to get Sinn Fein admitted to the talks in September.
Britain says Sinn Fein, which seeks to end British rule of Northern Ireland, can join the talks when they begin their substantive work in September providing the IRA truce is real.
But Trimble said the IRA might abandon its truce, as it did a previous ceasefire called in August 1994, if the talks do not lead to the end of British rule.
"It's very easy to turn off violence for a couple of weeks. The important thing is what do they intend. The worry is that this ceasefire is just as cynical as the last one," he said.

"I think it's very important that one probes the state of mind and the intentions of the leadership of Sinn Fein/IRA and it would be very helpful if they were to say simply that the war...is over and that they have no intention to resort to violence again and that they are going to commit themselves to a peaceful means of resolving our difficulties," he said.
Saturday's IRA ceasefire declaration pledged an unequivocal restoration of the previous, broken truce but made no mention of any end to the war against British rule.
The arms proposals apply to all political groups with guerrilla allies, including loyalist extremists already represented at the negotiations since an October 1994 ceasefire.

The proposals back "parallel decommissioning" as a way of breaking deadlock between unionists, who want the IRA to disarm to earn Sinn Fein a place at the talks, and Sinn Fein's stance that disarmament should be part of a final settlement.

Sinn Fein says the IRA, which sees itself as an anti-colonial guerrilla army, will not hand over a single bullet until a final settlement is reached which ends what it calls British occupation and leads to a withdrawal of Britain's army.

Decommissioning has divided the key protagonists since Britain and Ireland unveiled their "Downing Street Declaration" almost four years ago which promised a seat at peace talks to any group which repudiated violence.
